questions.question: Give an example of heat loss by each of conduction, convection and radiation, and explain why a windy day feels colder than a still day at the same temperature.
questions.expected_answer: Conduction: a person sitting on a cold concrete step loses heat into it. Convection: wind or moving air carries heat away from the body; warm air escapes through open windows. Radiation: the body radiates heat into a cold night sky. Wind blows away the thin layer of warm air next to the skin and replaces it with cold air, so heat is lost much faster by convection.

questions.question: Explain how a cool box and a vacuum flask reduce heat transfer by each method.
questions.expected_answer: Cool box: thick foam walls with trapped air slow conduction; a tight lid stops air flowing in and out, reducing convection; a white or light surface reflects sunlight, reducing radiation. Vacuum flask: the vacuum between the double walls stops conduction and convection because there are no particles; silvered surfaces reflect radiant heat; an insulating stopper slows heat loss through the top.

questions.question: Explain how ceiling insulation and layers of clothing keep people warm, and why birds fluff up their feathers.
questions.expected_answer: Ceiling insulation (fibreglass, polystyrene) traps still air, a poor conductor, and slows heat flow through the roof; foil under the roof reflects radiant heat; it keeps houses warmer in winter and cooler in summer. Several thin layers of clothing trap layers of still air next to the body, slowing heat loss; a windproof outer layer stops convection. Birds fluff up their feathers to trap a thicker layer of still air, which insulates better and slows heat loss from the body.
